recipes.title: Access request approval chain

description.need: A request nobody decided looks exactly like one that was denied, and the person waiting cannot tell which. Left alone, silence becomes the way privileged access gets granted.
description.input: A captured, classified request, the approval levels the organisation uses, and how long it has sat with its current approver.
description.core_action: Carry each request to an explicit approved, denied or escalated verdict, judging when a quiet approver has become an escalation and holding anything high privilege for a person to say yes out loud.
description.output: Every request carries a recorded decision, a decider and the time it took, and nothing is pending without a stated reason.

activities.label: Watch requests in flight and how long each has sat with its current approver
Put the request in front of the approver whose level it has reached
Decide whether a quiet approver needs a nudge or has become an escalation
Hold high privilege and sensitive requests for an explicit human decision
Record the verdict, who made it and how long it took
Tell the requestor where their request ended up

outcomes.statement: No access request sits without a decision or a clear reason it is still pending.
success_criteria: Every request reaches approved, denied or escalated within a window that matches its urgency
An approver falling behind is nudged before the request runs out of time
A request that runs out of time escalates rather than silently expiring

outcomes.statement: High privilege or sensitive access is never granted without an explicit human decision.
success_criteria: Admin level, production and sensitive resource requests always reach a human reviewer regardless of other automation
No approval is ever inferred from silence

recipes.guidance: Own getting every request to a clear, timely decision. Route through the configured levels, watch for approvers who have gone quiet, and escalate rather than let a request go silent. High privilege and sensitive requests always need an explicit human call. Use judgment on urgency and on who is worth nudging, but never auto advance past that gate. When approvers disagree or the escalation target is unclear, hand it to a person rather than guessing.

recommended_trigger.rationale: Two conditions drive this work and neither is a clock: a request arriving with its first approver, and a request approaching the point where its approver has gone quiet. Watching both directly is more honest than a poll, and lets an urgent request be chased sooner without reconfiguring anything.

personalization_needs: Which approval levels this organisation actually uses and who sits at each, since the chain shape is a property of the org rather than a default
What counts as high privilege here, because that line is the only thing standing between automation and an unreviewed grant
How long the adopter is willing to let a level hold a request before it is escalated, which is a rhythm judgment not a constant

input_schema.name: timeout_hours
input_schema.description: Standard-urgency approval timeout. Urgent halves it; emergency uses 4h.

input_schema.name: require_human_review_for_high_privilege
input_schema.description: Forces admin-level / production / sensitive resource requests through explicit human review regardless of other rules.

recipes.review_notes: v2 declared an empty connectors array, but its own description ("sends approval notifications"), its timeout reminder mechanic and its error handling ("Messages delivery failure, retry once") all evidence an outbound conversational channel, so connector_types is ["messaging"] rather than empty. This is inferred from the recipe's own text, not invented. "notifications" was considered and rejected: approval needs a reply from the approver and notifications connectors in this catalog are one way. The v2 suggested trigger was an event listener that "also wakes on a polling cadence to scan in-flight requests for timeouts", which is exactly the self_paced shape rather than either pure kind.
recipes.research_notes: Read the v2 prompt_template (including its errorHandling and reviewPolicy blocks) and the automation.json verdict, whose notes explain why this stays separate from intake. Compared the catalog membership of "messaging" (10 connectors, two way) against "notifications" (9, mostly one way webhooks) in scripts/connectors/builtin to pick the type.

recipes.title: Access grant audit and compliance reporting

description.need: When somebody asks why an access grant was approved, the answer is usually reconstructed by hand from logs, months late, by whoever still remembers. Approval bottlenecks stay invisible in the same way, buried inside an average.
description.input: The ledger of access requests, their approvers, their verdicts and how long each level held them.
description.core_action: Turn one ledger into both the periodic account and any point in time compliance answer, so the two can never disagree, and name the approvers who are slowing the chain instead of letting an average hide them.
description.output: A standing, defensible record of who asked, who decided and how long it took, with bottlenecks named and any gap in the source stated.

activities.label: Read the access request ledger across the period in question
Check the ledger against what the approval work actually recorded
Aggregate volumes, verdicts and time to decision
Name the approvers whose response times are dragging the chain
Compose the account, stating any gap in the source plainly
Deliver the account and answer point in time compliance questions from the same ledger

outcomes.statement: Anyone asking why an access grant was approved can get the full chain of approvals and justification for any date range without a person digging through logs.
success_criteria: A compliance answer for any requested date range reconstructs every grant with its approver, justification and timing
No follow up question about a specific grant requires manual log diving

outcomes.statement: Approval bottlenecks are visible to the team before they become a recurring complaint.
success_criteria: The periodic account names the approver with the slowest average response time, not just an aggregate
Time to decision is comparable across consecutive periods

recipes.guidance: Own the standing record of who asked, who decided, how long it took and whether the pattern is healthy. Produce the periodic rollup and any compliance answer from the same ledger so the two never disagree. Call out approvers who are consistently slow rather than burying them in an average. If the source is unreadable, still ship a partial account and say what is missing rather than going quiet.

recommended_trigger.rationale: Two conditions, neither a clock: enough approval activity has accumulated to say something the last account did not, or a compliance question has been asked. No statutory calendar forces a date here, so a cadence would only manufacture accounts into periods where nothing moved.

personalization_needs: Who reads this and what decision they make with it, since that sets the length and the shape entirely
What the adopter's regulator or auditor actually asks for, because a compliance answer is only defensible against a real question
What counts as too slow for an approver here, which is a rhythm judgment and not a fixed number
dependencies: An access request ledger already being written by the intake work; this recipe reads that record and does not create it

input_schema.name: audit_enabled
input_schema.description: Whether every request generates a compliance-grade audit record. Disabling not recommended for regulated industries.

recipes.review_notes: Retitled from "Audit & Reporting", which named neither an area nor an activity. v2 carried three cadences (daily digest, weekly summary, on demand report) in one recipe; v3 keeps the job and drops all three, since the spec forbids a cadence on a recipe and the lane rule only allows time where a statutory calendar forces it, which nothing here does. The dependency on an upstream ledger is real and evidenced by v2 error handling ("Audit DB unreadable, reconstruct from in-flight buffer"), so it is declared rather than assumed.
recipes.research_notes: Read the v2 prompt_template and the reporting.json verdict for this id. Checked the lane rule for legal_compliance in the brief against the v2 cron, and checked the Contractor responsibility "A current account of where things stand" in convert_B.json as the corpus precedent for a self_paced account ("do not produce an account into a period where nothing moved"), which is the same shape.

recipes.title: Access request intake and triage

description.need: Access requests arrive as ordinary messages among everything else, so the same ask gets entered twice, or read once and forgotten, and the record of who asked for what stops being something anyone would defend.
description.input: Inbound request messages, the organisation's own access level vocabulary, and the record of requests already captured.
description.core_action: Decide what each message is really asking for, whether it has already been captured, and how much privilege it carries, because that classification is what later decides whether a person has to say yes.
description.output: One durable, deduplicated request record per real ask, classified by privilege and ready for a decision.

activities.label: Collect inbound access requests from the watched channel
Read the requestor, resource, access level and urgency out of each message
Set aside repeats and messages from senders who may not ask
Judge privilege level against the organisation's own access vocabulary
Write each real request as a durable audit record
Hand the classified request to the approval decision

outcomes.statement: Every incoming access request is captured once, correctly classified, and never lost.
success_criteria: Each distinct request produces exactly one audit record, with duplicates and malformed requests handled without dropping the underlying ask
Every request carries an accurate privilege classification before it reaches the approval chain

outcomes.statement: The approval chain never starts deciding on an incomplete or unverified request.
success_criteria: Requests from unverified or external senders are flagged rather than queued for approval
The audit record exists and is durable before the approval work is notified

recipes.guidance: Own turning inbound access requests into a queue the approval work can trust. Extract the real ask from each message, catch duplicates and malformed requests, and classify privilege carefully, since that classification decides whether a person must review later. Completeness and correctness of the record matter more than speed. Never hand a request onward before its record is durable, and flag an unverified sender rather than queueing them.

recommended_trigger.rationale: A request arriving is a real external occurrence and the work has no value before it. Adoption may realise this as inbox polling where the bound connector cannot push, but the kind of thing being waited on is an arrival, not a clock.

personalization_needs: The organisation's access level vocabulary, because privilege classification is the whole judgment here and the words differ per organisation
Which inbox, label or folder carries real requests, since the seat should not read everything
Who counts as allowed to ask, because a request from outside is a security signal rather than a queue item

input_schema.name: approval_levels
input_schema.description: Shape of the approval chain the intake primes; drives how many levels the audit record anticipates.

input_schema.name: access_level_scheme
input_schema.description: Organization's access-level vocabulary (e.g., 'Read-only, Write, Admin' or 'Viewer, Editor, Owner'). Used to classify the requested level and flag high-privilege tiers.

No vendor is evidenced anywhere in the source, so examples is empty rather than populated with a guess.

Checked _lanes_v3.json: superseded_by is empty for this id, so the consolidation verdict is the authority.

recipes.title: Contract intake and risk analysis

description.need: Contracts get signed on the strength of whoever had time to read them. Unfavourable terms, missing protections and clauses that are out of line with what this counterparty has signed before go unmentioned because nobody compared.
description.input: An incoming contract document, the team's stated risk tolerance, and the reviewed history of the same counterparty.
description.core_action: Judge the contract on terms, money, obligations and risk, with this counterparty's own prior contracts as the market baseline, and refuse to analyse a document that is unreadable, partial, or an amendment whose original is missing.
description.output: A structured review a person can act on without rereading the contract, with every market claim traceable to a real prior contract.

activities.label: Take in an incoming contract and get readable text out of it
Decide whether the document is complete enough to analyse at all
Identify the contract type and pull the counterparty's own history
Work through key terms, financials and obligations
Judge risk, red flags and how the terms sit against what this counterparty signed before
Produce the structured review and the dates it commits anyone to

outcomes.statement: Nobody signs or acts on a contract whose unfavourable terms, missing protections or red flags were never surfaced.
success_criteria: Every intake worthy contract produces a structured review covering key terms, financials, obligations, risk, red flags and market comparison before anyone is expected to act on it
A contract that cannot be confidently classified, reads suspiciously short, or references an original the seat does not have, is routed to a person rather than analysed as if complete

outcomes.statement: A claim like "this escalation clause is above market" can be traced back to the counterparty's own contract history rather than asserted from nothing.
success_criteria: Market comparison language cites the counterparty's prior reviewed contracts wherever any exist
A comparison made with no prior history says so instead of implying a baseline

recipes.guidance: Own turning an incoming contract into a review someone can act on without rereading the source. Classify it, then work through terms, money, obligations, risk and market position with the counterparty's own history as context. Escalate rather than guess when the document is unreadable, encrypted, partial, or an amendment without its original. Match strictness to the risk tolerance the team stated, not to a personal bar.

recommended_trigger.rationale: A contract arriving is a real external occurrence with a deadline attached to it, and there is no work to do before one arrives. v2 already offered both a poll and a webhook for the same arrival, which is the tell that the arrival, not the interval, is the thing.

personalization_needs: Which contract types this team actually reviews, because that decides which clause patterns and risk factors the reading emphasises
Where contracts arrive and how they are marked, since the seat should not read an entire inbox
How strict the team wants to be, because the same clause is a red flag under one tolerance and normal under another
Whether an unreadable document should be bounced back to the sender or held quietly, which is a relationship decision

input_schema.name: contract_types
input_schema.description: Which contract types the team reviews most often , informs which clause patterns and risk factors the analysis emphasizes.

input_schema.name: risk_tolerance
input_schema.description: Conservative flags anything non-standard; moderate flags unfavorable + missing protections; aggressive only flags critical risks.

Confirmed no OCR or PDF dependency appears anywhere in the source before leaving dependencies empty.

recipes.title: Contract obligation and deadline watch

description.need: A contract's consequences are carried by dates that live inside it: notice windows, obligation due dates, warranty expiries. Nobody re-reads a signed contract to find them, so they arrive as surprises.
description.input: Every tracked contract with the dates it carries, and the record of which of those dates have already been raised.
description.core_action: Decide which dates are close enough to matter, how urgent each has become, and who can actually act, without raising the same date at the same urgency twice.
description.output: No date with a consequence passes without the person who could have acted on it having been told while there was still time.

activities.label: Survey every tracked contract obligation and the date attached to it
Judge which dates are close enough to matter and how urgent each has become
Set aside dates already raised at the same urgency
Raise the date with the people who can act on it
Escalate a date that keeps being raised and keeps being ignored
Record what was raised so the next pass does not repeat it

outcomes.statement: Nobody is surprised by a contract renewal, termination window, obligation or warranty deadline arriving unannounced.
success_criteria: Every tracked date is raised at each level of urgency before it lapses
A date already raised at a given urgency is never raised again at that same urgency
A date that passed without anybody acting is treated as a miss regardless of whether the message was delivered

recipes.guidance: Own visibility into every date a signed contract commits someone to: renewals, notice windows, obligations, warranties. Reach the people who can act, size the urgency to how near the date is, and never repeat yourself at the same level. A date that passed with nobody acting is a miss even if the message went out. A date that is consistently ignored is a pattern to escalate, not a reminder to send again.

recommended_trigger.rationale: The dates themselves are what is watched, and each contract has its own. A daily sweep is one way to notice them but it is not the thing being noticed, and it wakes the seat on days when nothing is near. Nothing statutory forces a calendar here.

personalization_needs: Which dates this adopter tracks and where they are recorded, since a deadline nobody wrote down cannot be watched
Who can actually act on each kind of date, because a reminder that reaches the wrong person looks handled and is not
How far ahead a date should be raised, which differs sharply between a notice window and a warranty expiry

input_schema.name: reminder_recipients
input_schema.description: Comma-separated additional email recipients for deadline reminders (besides the original submitter).

examples.title: Gmail as the reminder channel
examples.notes: v2 sent the reminder to the original submitter plus a configured list. On Gmail a bounce is the failure that matters: v2 learned to leave the reminder unmarked so the next pass retries it rather than recording a send that never landed.

recipes.research_notes: Read the v2 prompt_template and the content.json verdict including its disambiguation note naming all four near identical source titles. Cross read 2d6945b7 and 55bf5308 in this same lane to keep the three scopes genuinely disjoint (signatures, renewal clock, everything else a signed contract commits you to).

recipes.title: Contract review publication and risk alert

description.need: A completed contract review that only exists inside the reviewer helps nobody. The submitter chases for a verdict, and legal either hears about every routine contract or about none of the risky ones.
description.input: A finished structured contract review with its risk level, its flags and the dates it found.
description.core_action: Decide who this finding is for: publish it where contract records already live, give the submitter a verdict they can act on, and pull legal in only when severity or flag count crosses the line the team drew.
description.output: The analysis is on the record, the submitter knows what happens next, and legal was interrupted exactly when it was worth interrupting.

activities.label: Take a completed contract review as it lands
Publish the full analysis where the team already looks for contract records
Tell the submitter what was found and what happens next
Weigh flag count and severity against the line the team drew
Pull legal in when that line is crossed, and leave them alone when it is not
Update the contract record and the dates it now carries

outcomes.statement: The person who submitted a contract knows what was found and what happens next without chasing anyone.
success_criteria: Every submitter receives a summary after their contract is reviewed
The summary states the risk level and the specific flags behind it, not just a score

outcomes.statement: Legal is pulled in immediately when a contract is genuinely risky, and not for routine ones.
success_criteria: Every contract crossing the high risk threshold or carrying any critical flag reaches the legal channel
Legal is not paged for contracts below the threshold

recipes.guidance: Convert a completed review into the record of what was found and the news for whoever needs it. Publish the full analysis, tell the submitter plainly, and pull legal in only when the count or the severity crosses the line the team set. Treat a publishing or messaging failure as recoverable: keep the analysis and retry rather than losing a finding that took real work to produce.

recommended_trigger.rationale: This work exists only in response to a review completing, and has nothing to do between reviews. Waking on the completion is the whole of it.

personalization_needs: Where this team already keeps contract records, since publishing into a place nobody reads is the same as not publishing
What the team counts as high risk, because that line is what protects legal from being paged for routine work
Whether outbound summaries to external submitters need a person to see them first

input_schema.name: legal_team_channel
input_schema.description: messaging channels for high-risk alerts (e.g., #legal-review).

input_schema.name: high_risk_threshold

recipes.title: Support issue disposition account

description.need: Whoever is accountable for a support queue cannot tell from the tracker whether it was handled or merely touched. Without a short account they either open the tracker themselves or stop asking.
description.input: What actually happened to issues since the last account, and the counts the source itself reports.
description.core_action: Say what happened to the issues that were touched, reconciled against the source rather than against local state, and pick the few worth naming instead of counting everything.
description.output: A short account anyone accountable can read without opening the tracker, honest about any gap in the data behind it.

activities.label: Gather what happened to issues since the last account
Reconcile the counts against the source rather than local state alone
Decide which issues are worth naming rather than counting
Compose a short account that states any gap in the data plainly
Deliver it where the people accountable will actually read it

outcomes.statement: The seat can account for what happened to every issue it touched, without anyone reconstructing it from the tracker.
success_criteria: Each issue named carries its last action and what it is waiting on
Counts reported about the backlog reconcile with the source rather than with local state alone
A gap in the underlying data is stated plainly rather than presented as a confident number

outcomes.statement: The people accountable for the queue stay current on it without opening the tracker.
success_criteria: The account is short enough to be read in full
Every issue linked from it resolves to a real, currently valid ticket

recipes.guidance: Own a trustworthy account of how the reported issues were handled. Turn recent triage activity into something people can act on without opening the tracker, and reconcile your counts against the source rather than your own notes. When the underlying data is incomplete, say so plainly rather than presenting confident numbers. Keep it short enough that people actually read it, and link out to notable issues instead of restating them.

recommended_trigger.rationale: Act when enough has happened to be worth saying, or when someone asks. A daily cron produces an account into days where nothing moved, which is exactly how a digest becomes something people stop reading.

personalization_needs: Who reads this and what they decide with it, which sets the length and shape entirely
Which queue or project this account covers, since one account over several queues is a different job
How much movement is worth an account here, because that threshold is what keeps it from becoming noise

recipes.title: Issue source coverage and triage

description.need: A reported issue that nobody looked at again is indistinguishable from one that was handled. Over time the tracker fills with things that are old rather than things that are open, and nobody trusts it enough to read it.
description.input: One tracked issue source, the issues created or updated since the last pass, and the set of solutions already known to work.
description.core_action: Judge whether each issue holds real work, attach a solution already known to work rather than restating the problem, and decide which issues need a person, reading tone and priority together rather than priority alone.
description.output: Nothing in the source is lost: everything with real work in it has reached the backlog in a shape that can be judged, and everything else has a stated reason it was closed.

activities.label: Advance coverage over the tracked source since the last pass
Judge whether each issue holds real work or should be closed with a reason
Look for a solution already known to work before proposing anything new
Attach a known solution, escalate what needs a person, or close what is abandoned
Promote what carries real work into the backlog in a shape that can be judged
Record what the outcome confirmed or contradicted so the known set improves

outcomes.statement: Nothing reported in the tracked source is lost, and everything with real work in it reaches the backlog in a shape that can be judged.
success_criteria: Coverage is continuous: every issue created or updated since the last pass has been seen
A promoted item carries the symptom, the affected area, and what is already known about it
The same issue is never promoted twice

outcomes.statement: An unhappy or high priority reporter always reaches a person, and is never auto closed into silence.
success_criteria: Tone and priority are read together, not priority alone, when deciding to escalate
Auto closing an abandoned issue reads as considerate rather than dismissive, and can be reopened

outcomes.statement: The set of known solutions becomes a more reliable source of fixes over time rather than a growing pile of guesses.
success_criteria: A confirmed resolution strengthens the entry that produced it
A rejected solution loses confidence so it stops being suggested

recipes.guidance: Own the completeness of one source so the operator never has to check it himself. Judge each issue on whether there is real work in it rather than on how loudly it was reported. Where a matching solution is already known, attach it instead of restating the problem, and only when you are genuinely confident. Bring anything ambiguous to a person rather than deciding on his behalf, and keep a promoted item small enough to act on.

recommended_trigger.rationale: Advance a cursor over the source rather than polling on a fixed interval: act when new or updated issues are plausibly waiting, and sooner when the previous pass left items unresolved. A fifteen minute cron rereads a quiet backlog and still lags a busy one.

personalization_needs: Which source, and which project or queue inside it, since the cut is one responsibility per source and each instance must know its slice
What makes an issue worth the backlog rather than worth closing, because that is the whole judgment and it differs completely between a bug tracker and a feedback inbox
Which known solutions may be attached without asking, because attaching a confident wrong answer to somebody else's issue is the expensive failure here
At what age silence should be read as abandonment here, since the source hard coded thirty days and that is a property of a team's rhythm

recipes.title: Memory and knowledge base health audit

description.need: The layers an agent remembers through decay quietly: notes go stale, documents orphan from the code they described, articles start disagreeing with each other. Nothing fails, and trust in the whole system erodes instead.
description.input: Whichever memory layers are configured, what each was last touched, and the totals from previous passes.
description.core_action: Find drift, staleness, orphans and contradiction, rank the findings by severity and recency, and hand every one to a person with a recommended action, never mutating a layer itself.
description.output: A capped, severity ranked set of findings queued for a human decision, and totals that let the next pass say whether it is getting better.

activities.label: Decide which memory layers are configured and in scope for this pass
Scan each layer for staleness, orphans and contradiction
Rank findings by severity and recency, capping rather than flooding the queue
Attach a recommended action to each finding
Queue every finding for a human decision, mutating nothing
Keep the totals so the next pass can say whether it is getting better

outcomes.statement: Stale, contradictory or orphaned content across the memory layers is caught and queued for a human decision rather than left to accumulate silently.
success_criteria: Every configured layer is audited and every finding reaches a person with a severity and a recommended action
Findings are capped sensibly per category with the suppressed count disclosed, not silently truncated
A deeper cross article contradiction pass runs at the scope the adopter wants, without needing a second charter to get it

outcomes.statement: The audit never changes a memory layer on its own.
success_criteria: Merge, archive, recompile and reduce importance are all decided by a person
A layer that is not configured is skipped and noted rather than failing the pass

recipes.guidance: Own catching drift, staleness, contradiction and orphaned content across the memory layers before it erodes trust in the system, and always let a person decide what to do about it; this work never mutates memory itself. Run the deeper cross article contradiction pass when the configured scope calls for it rather than treating it as a separate job. If a layer is not configured, skip it quietly and note it rather than failing.

recommended_trigger.rationale: Staleness accrues continuously and no external clock announces it. Act when enough content has changed or aged to be worth a pass, and take the deeper scope when the corpus has grown enough to warrant it. A weekly slot audits an unchanged corpus and misses a week of heavy writing.

personalization_needs: Which memory layers this adopter actually has, since a vault, a vector store and a persona memory each fail differently
What counts as stale here, because a reference note and a working note age at completely different rates
How many findings a person is willing to triage in one sitting, which is what the cap is really protecting
How deep a pass the adopter wants, since the contradiction scan costs materially more than the rest

input_schema.name: stale_threshold_days
input_schema.description: Days after which memories, KB documents, or vault notes without recent access count as stale. Matches the obsidian_brain_lint_vault default.

input_schema.name: max_issues_per_category
input_schema.description: Cap on findings per category per run. Prevents first-run explosions on old vaults.

input_schema.name: audit_scope
input_schema.description: Which layers to include. Vault audit is always auto-skipped when no vault is configured, regardless of this setting.

examples.title: Obsidian as an audited vault
examples.notes: v2 audited an optional Obsidian vault alongside persona memory and vector stores, and its rule was to skip the layer silently when no vault is configured rather than failing the pass. The reusable lesson is that a first pass over an old vault will find hundreds of things, which is why the per category cap exists at all.

recipes.title: Revenue signal alerting and outreach

description.need: Money that was going to arrive and did not, and accounts drifting toward leaving or ready to grow, all fail quietly. The window in which any of them can still be acted on is short, and by the time it shows up in a revenue report it has closed.
description.input: Signals crossing a threshold on a paying account, the record of which signals have already been raised, and whether the operator has agreed to any customer contact at all.
description.core_action: Separate a signal that will resolve on its own from one that needs a person, raise it once with its cause in the provider's own terms, and never contact a customer on the operator's behalf unless he has explicitly said that is wanted.
description.output: No revenue signal passes unnoticed, none is reported twice, and any outreach that went out is one the operator agreed to.

activities.label: Take a signal as it crosses its threshold
Separate a signal that will resolve on its own from one that needs a person
Check whether this account was already raised inside the suppression window
Alert the team and the account owner with the cause in the provider's own terms
Draft outreach matched to the situation, sending only where the operator has said that is wanted
Close a signal that resolved, and report repeats on one account as a pattern

outcomes.statement: Revenue is not lost to a signal that nobody saw.
success_criteria: A signal is raised once with its cause and attempt count rather than on every retry
A signal that resolves on its own is closed rather than left open
Repeated signals on one account are reported as a pattern

outcomes.statement: No customer hears from this seat unless the operator decided they should.
success_criteria: Outreach is drafted rather than sent wherever the adopter has not explicitly enabled sending
The same account is not contacted again inside the suppression window
Retention and expansion outreach read as different situations rather than one template

recipes.guidance: Own the money that was supposed to arrive and did not, and the accounts moving toward leaving or growing. Separate a transient signal the provider will resolve itself from one that needs a person, and involve the operator only for the second. Report the cause in the provider's own terms so it can be acted on. Do not contact a customer on his behalf unless he has explicitly said that is wanted, and respect the suppression window.

recommended_trigger.rationale: A threshold crossing is a real external occurrence with a short window in which it can still be recovered, so this wakes on the signal rather than pacing itself. Memory of what has already been raised is what stops a retrying provider from producing an alert per attempt.

personalization_needs: Whether the operator wants any customer contact at all from this seat, because the source template sent retention email automatically and that is a decision he has not made and must not be made for him
Which signals are worth interrupting a person over, since a provider that retries on its own produces many that are not
Who owns an account here, because an alert that reaches the wrong owner looks handled and is not

input_schema.name: outreach_mode
input_schema.description: auto_send = send retention + upgrade emails automatically when confidence > 0.70. draft_for_review = surface for owner approval first. alert_only = messaging only, never email.

recipes.title: Support escalation pattern review

description.need: A support function that only reports its escalations absorbs the same pain forever. The cause that produced fifty tickets is described fifty times and fixed never.
description.input: The escalation history far enough back to see a shape, the causes already filed as work, and what the last account said.
description.core_action: Name the causes behind recurring escalations rather than restating the escalations, decide which have a fixable root, and file those as work instead of reporting them again.
description.output: A short comparative account of what the escalations keep saying, with the fixable causes filed as work rather than described.

activities.label: Read the escalation history far enough back to see a shape
Name the causes behind recurring escalations rather than restating the escalations
Separate what changed from what has always been true, and skip causes already filed
File a cause with a fixable root as work
Give whoever is accountable a short comparative account, saying plainly when the product is at fault

outcomes.statement: A problem that keeps producing escalations gets fixed instead of escalated again.
success_criteria: Recurring causes are named and filed as work, not restated in each account
A cause already filed is not filed again each time it recurs
A pattern that is getting worse is escalated rather than waited on

outcomes.statement: The person accountable sees what changed, not a repeat of numbers they have already read.
success_criteria: The account distinguishes what changed from what has always been true
Repeat requesters and unusually long waits are called out by name rather than buried in an average
It is short enough to be read at the end of a long day

recipes.guidance: Read your own escalation history for patterns and turn the ones with a fixable cause into work. This is the difference between a support seat that absorbs pain forever and one that reduces it. Say plainly when the pattern is the product's fault. Keep the account short and comparative, because the useful content is what changed, and escalate a pattern that is getting worse rather than waiting to report it.

recommended_trigger.rationale: Act when enough escalations have accumulated to see a shape, or when one cause has recurred often enough to be worth naming. A fixed evening slot produces an account on days with nothing to say, which is how a digest trains its reader to skip it.

personalization_needs: Where filed causes should go, since a backlog and a knowledge base serve different follow up
Who reads this account and what decision they make with it, which sets its length and shape
How far back the adopter considers relevant, because pattern detection over the wrong window invents trends

input_schema.name: lead_email
input_schema.description: Recipient of the daily HTML digest.

input_schema.name: trend_alert_threshold
input_schema.description: Percent of 7-day avg above which the digest generates recommendations.

examples.title: Notion as the escalation record

Naming the gap is what keeps a pattern claim honest, since a pattern read off an incomplete window is worse than no pattern.

recipes.title: Support request SLA watch and escalation

description.need: Somebody who asked for help is waiting, and nobody knows it. A breach discovered after the fact is only a report; the same information an hour earlier would have been a save.
description.input: The open request queue with what was promised on each, how long each has waited, and the history of who has been escalated for what.
description.core_action: Judge which requests are entering their risk window before they breach, and which genuinely need a person, since escalating everything is as bad as escalating nothing.
description.output: Nobody who asked for help is waiting without either an answer or a human knowing they are waiting, and every escalation carries enough context that nobody rebuilds the case.

activities.label: Watch the oldest unanswered request and any commitment coming due
Judge which requests are entering their risk window before they breach it
Decide what genuinely needs a person, since escalating everything is as bad as escalating nothing
Enrich the case with repeat requester and agent load context so a pattern is visible
Escalate with enough context to decide, and hand over one account when many break at once
Log every escalation so later pattern work has something real to read

outcomes.statement: Nobody who asked for help is waiting without either an answer or a human knowing they are waiting.
success_criteria: The oldest unanswered request is always known, and the seat can say why it is still open
A request entering its risk window is warned about before it breaches, not only after
A request escalated once is not escalated again for the same reason

outcomes.statement: The most urgent cases reach a person directly rather than a channel that might be missed, and routine ones do not.
success_criteria: What was promised to a requester is tracked against what actually happened
When many requests break at once, one account of the situation is handed over rather than a stream of alerts

outcomes.statement: Repeat requesters and overloaded agents show up as patterns the team can act on, not as isolated escalations.
success_criteria: An escalation notes when the same requester or issue has recurred
Every escalation is logged somewhere later pattern analysis can read

recipes.guidance: Hold the promise made to whoever asked. Answer what you can answer well, and put in front of a person what needs one, with enough context that they do not have to reconstruct the case. The judgment is in deciding what genuinely needs a person: escalating everything is as bad as escalating nothing. Warn before the breach rather than after. When many things break at once, hand over one account rather than a stream of alerts.

recommended_trigger.rationale: What is watched is a clock condition the seat can hold itself: the oldest unanswered request, and any commitment about to come due. Act sooner when something is time sensitive and later when the queue is quiet, rather than polling every two minutes through the night. The request arriving is an event, but the waiting is not.

personalization_needs: What the adopter has actually promised requesters, since urgency is meaningless without a commitment to measure it against
Which situations require a person and which the seat may answer alone, which is a trust boundary only the adopter can set
How the adopter wants to be reached when something needs them, and what is important enough to interrupt for
Which requester tiers are in scope, because silencing a tier is a deliberate business choice rather than a filter
dependencies: Response commitments defined in the support platform, since a wait has nothing to be measured against otherwise

superseded_by: Nothing waits longer than it should

lane_findings: One connector token in this lane has NO matching catalog category: "legal" (recipes 4d115a03 and 2d6945b7, both from contract-lifecycle-use-case). All 48 categories values across the 134 files in scripts/connectors/builtin were enumerated; there is no legal, esignature, contract or agreement category, and no docusign, adobe-sign, hellosign or pandadoc connector. "forms" is used as the nearest (a document sent out for a counterparty to complete and return, with a webhook on completion, which is what formbricks and tally model) but it is a stretch. The right fix is an esignature category with a real connector behind it; until then adoption cannot bind these two recipes at all.

The "support" category is real but carried by exactly ONE connector (crisp). Two recipes in this lane declare it (410bed86, 70e00cca), so the type resolves to a single choice at adoption, which defeats the point of a type. Zendesk, Freshdesk, Intercom and Help Scout are all absent from the catalog. This is a catalog gap rather than a recipe problem.

Twelve of the twenty ids are superseded, but only nine distinct designed responsibilities cover them, because three responsibilities each supersede two recipes: App Master "Keeping the open issue set from rotting" (0b13d1e5 and 26b22f83), Contractor "No date passes unnoticed" (2d6945b7 and 55bf5308), and Database owner "Answering questions against live data without putting it at risk" (34e0d640 and d227eebc). In each case the responsibility's success criteria split cleanly and both ids are preserved per the brief, but each pair is now much closer than it was, because the cadence was often the only thing separating them. Phase D should decide the merges deliberately rather than inherit three near duplicates.

Removing the cadence is what exposed the duplication. Nine of the twenty recipes were named or scoped by their clock ("Weekly Query Digest", "Monthly Deep Audit", "Daily Escalation Digest", "48-hour" style titles, "Support Digest" against "Issue Health Report"). Once the cron comes off, several pairs describe the same job at two intervals. This is the strongest argument in this lane for the v3 shape and also the largest cleanup it creates.

The trigger split is 6 event, 14 self_paced, 0 time. Nothing in this lane produced a genuine time trigger: no statutory calendar was found anywhere in legal_compliance (the dates are per contract, not per jurisdiction), every SLA and reminder loop is a clock CONDITION the seat can watch, and every digest cadence was an authoring convenience rather than an external requirement. If a downstream reviewer expects any recipe corpus to contain time triggers, this lane is evidence that the honest answer is often none.

input_schema carried verbatim collides with connector_types in one place: 34e0d640 declares a connector_ref knob (target_database, ui_component DatabaseSelector, connector "database") that is the v2 way of doing exactly what connector_types plus AdoptionAnswers.credential_bindings now do. It is carried per the brief, but Phase C1 should reconcile the two seams rather than ship both.

One character was changed inside a verbatim input_schema: efb53700's contract_types description contained the only em dash in any of the twenty schemas, normalised to a comma so the file satisfies the house rule. Every other input_schema is byte identical to its v2 source. Disclosed here rather than left silent.

Vendor substitution artifacts survived in two titles and were removed: "legal platform Event Processing" (4d115a03) and "knowledge base Publish and Risk Alert" (04756772). Both are cases where a redacted vendor was replaced by its category and the result was left in a title, which then reads as neither an area nor a vendor. The pattern to look for elsewhere in the corpus is a lowercase category word sitting in title case position.

Two ids carry a real prerequisite that adoption must verify rather than install: 4d115a03 needs a delivery endpoint the signature platform can reach, and 410bed86 needs response commitments actually defined in the support platform, since a wait has nothing to measure against otherwise. Everything else in the lane evidenced no dependency, and none was invented; eighteen of twenty have an empty dependencies array.

d4388f24 sits between two domains and the lane roster and the superseding responsibility disagree. The roster and the consolidation verdict file it under customer_support; the superseding Web marketer responsibility "Failed collection watch" is filed under finance_accounting. The roster is followed here so the lane counts hold, but this is a real disagreement about which seat owns revenue signals and it should be settled rather than inherited.
